Content:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is called reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for every element [MATH: x \in A.] In other words, each element of [MATH: A] is related to itself by [MATH: R.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- Any integer [MATH: x] is congruent to itself modulo [MATH: n] for any natural [MATH: n.]
[MATH: x\equiv x \quad(\textrm{mod } n)]
So, congruence of integers is reflexive.
- The relation "are born in the same year," defined on the set containing the entire human population, is also reflexive. This is because any person was born in the same year as themselves.

Content:
A binary relation [MATH: R] on a set [MATH: A] is called irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \notin R] for every element [MATH: x \in A.] In other words, no element of [MATH: A] is related to itself by [MATH: R.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The relation "is less than" [MATH: (\lt),] defined on the set of real numbers, is irreflexive since no number is less than itself. In other words, the statement
[MATH: x < x]
is false for any [MATH: x\in\mathbb R.]

Content:
- The relation "is the sisters of," defined on the set containing all people, is irreflexive. This is because a person can't be their own sister.

Content:
A relation cannot be both reflexive and irreflexive simultaneously. However, most relations are neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

Content:
For example, consider relation [MATH: x \: R \: y,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] as [MATH: xy \lt 10{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: R] is not reflexive since [MATH: 5 \cdot 5 \not\lt 10,] which means that [MATH: 5] is not related to itself.
- [MATH: R] is not irreflexive since [MATH: 1 \cdot 1 \lt 10,] which means that [MATH: 1] is related to itself.

Content:
Let's describe the properties of adjacency matrices for reflexive and irreflexive relations.

Content:
- A finite binary relation is reflexive if and only if its adjacency matrix has only [MATH: 1]'s on the main diagonal (from top-left to bottom-right).

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,1), (1,2), (2,2), (3,3) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is reflexive, and its adjacency matrix is the following:

Content:
| | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] |

Content:
- A finite binary relation is irreflexive if and only if its adjacency matrix has only [MATH: 0]'s on the main diagonal.

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is irreflexive, and its adjacency matrix is the following:

Content:
| | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] |

Content:
For relations that are neither reflexive nor irreflexive, the corresponding adjacency matrix will have both [MATH: 0]'s and [MATH: 1]'s on the main diagonal.

[MATH: R = \big\{ (-2,-2), (-2,0), (0,0), (2,-2), (2,0) \big\}]

sections.readable_text:
Consider the following relation defined on the set [MATH: A = \{ -2,0,2 \}.]

[MATH: R = \big\{ (-2,-2), (-2,0), (0,0), (2,-2), (2,0) \big\}]

Determine whether the relation is reflexive, irreflexive, or neither.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is

  • reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for all [MATH: x \in A,]

  • irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) otin R] for all [MATH: x \in A.]

If some pairs of the form [MATH: (x,x)] belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

In our case, the relation is defined on [MATH: \{ -2,0,2 \},] and we have

[MATH: (-2,-2) \in R, \qquad (0,0) \in R, \qquad (2,2) otin R.]

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

[MATH: \qquad] Since [MATH: (2,2) otin R] and [MATH: (0,0) \in R,] the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.
sections.readable_text:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is

- reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for all [MATH: x \in A,]
- irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \notin R] for all [MATH: x \in A.]

If some pairs of the form [MATH: (x,x)] belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

In our case, the relation is defined on [MATH: \{ -2,0,2 \},] and we have

[MATH: (-2,-2) \in R, \qquad
(0,0) \in R, \qquad
(2,2) \notin R.]

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

[MATH: \qquad] Since [MATH: (2,2) \notin R] and [MATH: (0,0) \in R,] the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is

- reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for all [MATH: x \in A,]
- irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \notin R] for all [MATH: x \in A.]

If some pairs of the form [MATH: (x,x)] belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

In our case, the relation is defined on [MATH: \{ -2,0,2 \},] and we have

[MATH: (-2,-2) \in R, \qquad
(0,0) \in R, \qquad
(2,2) \notin R.]

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

[MATH: \qquad] Since [MATH: (2,2) \notin R] and [MATH: (0,0) \in R,] the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

sections.normalized_html:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is

  • reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for all [MATH: x \in A,]

  • irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \notin R] for all [MATH: x \in A.]

If some pairs of the form [MATH: (x,x)] belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation [MATH: R] is reflexive. Indeed, [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{Z}.] Notice that [MATH: 2\mid (x+x)] for any [MATH: x \in \mathbb{Z}.]

  • Relation [MATH: S] is irreflexive. Indeed, [MATH: (x,x) \notin S] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{Z}.] Notice that [MATH: x \mid x] for any [MATH: x \in \mathbb{Z}.]

  • Relation [MATH: T] is neither reflexive nor irreflexive. Notice that

    • [MATH: (1,1) \notin T] since [MATH: 3 \not \mid (1^2+1),] while

    • [MATH: (0,0) \in T] since [MATH: 3 \mid (0^2+0).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: R] only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is called reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for every element [MATH: x \in A.] In other words, each element of [MATH: A] is related to itself by [MATH: R.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- Any integer [MATH: x] is congruent to itself modulo [MATH: n] for any natural [MATH: n.]
[MATH: x\equiv x \quad(\textrm{mod } n)]
So, congruence of integers is reflexive.
- The relation "are born in the same year," defined on the set containing the entire human population, is also reflexive. This is because any person was born in the same year as themselves.

Content:
A binary relation [MATH: R] on a set [MATH: A] is called irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \notin R] for every element [MATH: x \in A.] In other words, no element of [MATH: A] is related to itself by [MATH: R.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The relation "is less than" [MATH: (\lt),] defined on the set of real numbers, is irreflexive since no number is less than itself. In other words, the statement
[MATH: x < x]
is false for any [MATH: x\in\mathbb R.]

Content:
- The relation "is the sisters of," defined on the set containing all people, is irreflexive. This is because a person can't be their own sister.

Content:
A relation cannot be both reflexive and irreflexive simultaneously. However, most relations are neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

Content:
For example, consider relation [MATH: x \: R \: y,] defined on [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] as [MATH: xy \lt 10{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: R] is not reflexive since [MATH: 5 \cdot 5 \not\lt 10,] which means that [MATH: 5] is not related to itself.
- [MATH: R] is not irreflexive since [MATH: 1 \cdot 1 \lt 10,] which means that [MATH: 1] is related to itself.

Content:
We can summarize all the above in the following diagram:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/749accff81069e12976cbe99a1879b56]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Adjacency Matrices of Reflexive and Irreflexive Relations

Content:
Let's describe the properties of adjacency matrices for reflexive and irreflexive relations.

Content:
- A finite binary relation is reflexive if and only if its adjacency matrix has only [MATH: 1]'s on the main diagonal (from top-left to bottom-right).

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,1), (1,2), (2,2), (3,3) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is reflexive, and its adjacency matrix is the following:

Content:
| | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}] |

Content:
- A finite binary relation is irreflexive if and only if its adjacency matrix has only [MATH: 0]'s on the main diagonal.

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is irreflexive, and its adjacency matrix is the following:

Content:
| | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] |

Content:
For relations that are neither reflexive nor irreflexive, the corresponding adjacency matrix will have both [MATH: 0]'s and [MATH: 1]'s on the main diagonal.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Reflexive and Irreflexive Relations

Example Prompt:
Consider the following relation defined on the set [MATH: A = \{ -2,0,2 \}.]

[MATH: R = \big\{ (-2,-2), (-2,0), (0,0), (2,-2), (2,0) \big\}]

Determine whether the relation is reflexive, irreflexive, or neither.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A binary relation [MATH: R,] defined on a set [MATH: A,] is

- reflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \in R] for all [MATH: x \in A,]
- irreflexive if [MATH: (x,x) \notin R] for all [MATH: x \in A.]

If some pairs of the form [MATH: (x,x)] belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

In our case, the relation is defined on [MATH: \{ -2,0,2 \},] and we have

[MATH: (-2,-2) \in R, \qquad
(0,0) \in R, \qquad
(2,2) \notin R.]

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

[MATH: \qquad] Since [MATH: (2,2) \notin R] and [MATH: (0,0) \in R,] the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Plots of Reflexive and Irreflexive Relations

Content:
Plots of reflexive and irreflexive relations have the following properties:

Content:
- A binary relation is reflexive if and only if its plot contains all the corresponding points on the line [MATH: y=x.]

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,1), (1,2), (2,2), (3,3) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is reflexive, and its plot contains all the diagonal points, as shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d402951059ae634ae27f27c9095d9e05]

Content:
- A binary relation is irreflexive if and only if its plot does not contain any points on the line [MATH: y=x.]

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is irreflexive, and its plot does not contain any diagonal points, as shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9cf2a3f2ad429e2f5f325692f041efde]

Content:
For relations that are neither reflexive nor irreflexive, the corresponding plot will have some points on the line [MATH: y=x] but not all of them.

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: Digraphs of Reflexive and Irreflexive Relations

Content:
Digraphs of reflexive and irreflexive relations have the following properties:

Content:
- A binary relation is reflexive if and only if its digraph has a loop at every node.

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,1), (1,2), (2,2), (3,3) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is reflexive, and its digraph has a loop at each node, as shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2f4286399992b175e13c83c3da0404f7]

Content:
- A binary relation is irreflexive if and only if its digraph does not contain any loops at the nodes.

For example, the relation [MATH: R = \big\{ (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2) \big\},] defined on [MATH: \{1,2,3\},] is irreflexive, and its digraph has no loops, as shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f5bbbc77d9e641ba6aa803dae46be779]

Content:
For relations that are neither reflexive nor irreflexive, the corresponding digraph will have loops at some nodes but not at all of them.
